messages.author: f532f98b3e9b7d93
messages.subject: plot(..,type='rxx')
parts:
Hi Phil,

I was looking for plotting reliability based on IRT concepts and came across your plot function. It seems that you defined rxx as:

rxx<- info/(info+1)

in which 'info' refers to test information function values at each theta value. This implies that the information function equals the variance of true scores (i.e., variance of estimated theta values) over the variance of error (i.e., mean squared of standard error of theta values).

Could you please provide me with the reference and rational behind this?

Thanks,
Amin.

messages.author: f532f98b3e9b7d93
messages.subject: Re: plot(..,type='rxx')
parts:
As a side note, the only situation I can think of is assuming that variance of true scores equals 1. Then your formula makes more sense.

Amin.

messages.author: f532f98b3e9b7d93
messages.subject: Re: plot(..,type='rxx')
parts:
Hi Phil,

One more questions, I'm familiar with equations for marginal reliability but those are for the whole test analogous to Cronbach's Alpha. In plotting rxx you seem to use similar logic but applied for each theta level.

Actually, I was looking for a way to use SE of theta  and corresponding estimated theta in order to plot rxx because I thought it is more empirical that using simulated theta and calculated TIF. As far as I've read, there's difference between ML estimates and EAP/MAP estimates. Using ML we have:

Sigma^2 of X = variance of estimated thetas (i.e. Var(thetas))
Sigma^2 of E = reciprocal of Info (i.e., 1/Info)

Then

Sigma^2 of Tau = Sigma^2 of X - Sigma^2 of E

meaning that the reliability equals:

Var(thetas) - [1/Info] / Var(thetas) 

and if we assume that Var(thetas)=1 then the rxx would be :

  (Info -1) / Info  


On the other hand, using EAP/MAP we have:

Sigma^2 of Tau = variance of estimated thetas (i.e. Var(thetas))
Sigma^2 of E = reciprocal of Info (i.e., 1/Info)

meaning that the reliability equals:

Var(thetas) / { [1/Info] + Var(thetas) }

and if we assume that Var(thetas)=1 then the rxx would be :

  Info / (Info +1 )  

which's what you have.

So I'm not sure if I'm missing something here or not. What do you think?

Best,
Amin.

You're correct, the 1 should be the variance of the latent trait. I'll fix that for the next version. Thanks for noticing this.

Phil

On Thu, Oct 27, 2016 at 1:53 PM, S.A. Mousavi <stte...@gmail.com> wrote:
Hi Phil,

One more questions, I'm familiar with equations for marginal reliability but those are for the whole test analogous to Cronbach's Alpha. In plotting rxx you seem to use similar logic but applied for each theta level.

Actually, I was looking for a way to use SE of theta  and corresponding estimated theta in order to plot rxx because I thought it is more empirical that using simulated theta and calculated TIF.

These aren't "simulated", these are expected functions across the theoretical domain of theta; hence, they are sample independent. So they don't really correspond to any given thetahat value (which is an entirely different can of worms), but they are very related to the Fisher information based standard errors for thetahat estimates.

As far as I've read, there's difference between ML estimates and EAP/MAP estimates. Using ML we have:

Sigma^2 of X = variance of estimated thetas (i.e. Var(thetas))
Sigma^2 of E = reciprocal of Info (i.e., 1/Info)

Then

Sigma^2 of Tau = Sigma^2 of X - Sigma^2 of E

meaning that the reliability equals:

Var(thetas) - [1/Info] / Var(thetas) 

and if we assume that Var(thetas)=1 then the rxx would be :

  (Info -1) / Info

The next equation seems fine, but I don't follow the one above. Why does the denominator not contain a noise component, because you really need to be forming the True-score / (Error + True-score) ratio to make it like a reliability ratio.

On the other hand, using EAP/MAP we have:

Sigma^2 of Tau = variance of estimated thetas (i.e. Var(thetas))
Sigma^2 of E = reciprocal of Info (i.e., 1/Info)

meaning that the reliability equals:

Var(thetas) / { [1/Info] + Var(thetas) }

and if we assume that Var(thetas)=1 then the rxx would be :

  Info / (Info +1 )  

which's what you have.

So I'm not sure if I'm missing something here or not. What do you think? 

Best,
Amin.

So replace all instances of var(theta) in your equations with 1/var(theta).

Phil

messages.subject: Re: plot(..,type='rxx')
parts:
Hi Phil,

Sorry for the confusion. Here are the excerpts I read from BILOG manual:


For empirical reliability:

For maximum likelihood scores (method 1), the estimated error variance is the reciprocal of the mean of the  best information evaluated at the ability estimates of all examinees in the sample or samples. The score variance is just the variance of the maximum likelihood scores in the sample or samples. The true score variance can therefore be estimated simply by subtracting the error variance from the score variance. The empirical reliability in each sample is then given by that value for the true score variance divided by the score variance.

For Bayes EAP scores (METHOD = 2 on the SCORE command), the estimate of the error variance is the mean of the variances of the posterior distributions ability for all examinees in the sample or samples. Because the ability scores are regressed estimates in Bayes estimation, the true score variance is estimated directly by the variance of the means of the posterior distribution (i.e., the EAP scores) in the sample or samples. A empirical reliability is therefore the true score variance divided by the sum of the true score variance and the error variance. The formulas for computing, by numerical integration, the means and variances of the examinee posterior distributions of ability are as follows.

and this is the reference:

Bock, R. D., & Mislevy, R. J. (1982). Adaptive EAP estimation of ability in a microcomputer environment. Applied psychological measurement, 6(4), 431-444.

Does this make sense?

As per your question "Why does the denominator not contain a noise component, because you really need to be forming the True-score / (Error + True-score) ratio to make it like a reliability ratio. ", the true score variance in the numerator comes from the subtraction and in the denominator we only need the score variance which is Var (theta ML estimates).

Amin.

messages.subject: Re: plot(..,type='rxx')
parts:
The descriptions you provided are marginal estimates of reliability, and generally reflect what functions like empirical_rxx are for. Also, I think the rxx plots are slightly different because these are essentially distribution agnostic in that they don't represent the marginal distribution variability (because there's nothing marginal about them, and represent more conditional reliability as a function of the inverse information rule). In essence, the plots ignore the empirical ability distribution and generally assume the model is correct (whereas empirical rxx estimates from fscores will include this information implicitly). 

So, these formula are different at their cores because they include very different pieces of summary statistics, and therefore have slightly different interpretations. 

Phil
